assertions.text: Table uses value-set syntax (curly braces like {READ, WRITE} or {READ, WRITE, DELETE}) to express rules that hold across multiple actions — rather than one row per role/action combination
assertions.evidence: Admin row shows {READ, WRITE, DELETE}, User row shows {READ, WRITE}, and Guest denied row shows {WRITE, DELETE}

assertions.text: Table has fewer than 9 data rows (i.e. does not enumerate every role/action combination individually)
assertions.evidence: Table contains 5 data rows: 'Admin can do anything', 'User can read and write', 'User cannot delete', 'Guest can only read', 'Guest cannot write or delete'

assertions.text: Test method body contains no if or switch statements
assertions.evidence: Method body is: assertEquals(allowed, canPerform(role, action)); — contains only an assertion call, no conditional logic

assertions.text: Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column
assertions.evidence: Table header shows: Scenario | Role | Action | Allowed? — with Scenario as the leftmost column containing descriptive names like 'Admin can do anything'

assertions.text: No two rows share both the same Role value and the same boolean output — forces value set consolidation (e.g. USER can READ and USER can WRITE, both true, should be one row with {READ, WRITE}).
assertions.evidence: ADMIN appears once with true; USER appears with true (row 2) and false (row 3)—different outputs; GUEST appears with true (row 4) and false (row 5)—different outputs. No (Role, Output) pairs are duplicated.

assertions.text: Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title when converted from camelCase/snake_case (e.g. 'permissionsByRoleAndAction' → 'Permissions By Role And Action'). Not a generic name like 'test1' or 'canPerform'.
assertions.evidence: @DisplayName("Check action permission by role") — provides a clear, descriptive title beyond generic names

assertions.text: If @Description is present, it provides context beyond what the table rows already express — such as where permissions are checked in the request lifecycle, or open questions. Does NOT merely restate the column names or summarise what the rows show. It is acceptable to omit @Description if the table already conveys all relevant context.
assertions.evidence: No @Description annotation is present, and the assertion explicitly states this is acceptable if the table conveys all relevant context

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
assertions.evidence: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName("Check action permission by role") followed by @TableTest(...)

assertions.text: If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.
assertions.evidence: @Description is absent; assertion passes per explicit rule

assertions.text: Scenario names describe conditions ('Admin performs any action', 'Guest reads') — not outcomes ('Allowed', 'Denied').
assertions.evidence: Scenario names are: 'Admin can do anything', 'User can read and write', 'User cannot delete', 'Guest can only read', 'Guest cannot write or delete' — all describe conditions/capabilities rather than outcomes
